days.title: Nationalisation
days.desc: Key industries and utilities, such as energy, water, rail or banking, are owned and run by the state rather than by private companies.
days.note: Putting industry in public hands is a left-wing idea. It says little about personal freedom, so it sits at the centre line.
days.source: Manifesto Project Dataset 2026a (Lehmann et al.), derived · 360 manifestos in 58 countries

days.title: Deregulating markets
days.desc: Removing or loosening government rules on business, such as licensing, price controls and workplace or environmental requirements, so firms have more freedom to operate.
days.note: Cutting red tape is a favourite of the economic right. It says little about personal freedom, so it stays close to the middle vertically.
days.source: CHES 2024 issue scores, derived (Rovny et al. 2025) · 24 parties in 18 countries

days.title: Self-reliance over welfare
days.desc: People and families look after themselves, with a smaller welfare state and lower taxes to pay for it.
days.note: Expecting people to look after themselves is the mirror image of redistribution. It sits well to the right, with a mild authoritarian tilt.
days.source: CHES 2024 issue scores, derived (Rovny et al. 2025) · 13 parties in 10 countries

days.title: Secular government
days.desc: Keeping religion separate from the state, so that laws and public institutions are not based on any one faith.
days.note: Keeping religion out of lawmaking is backed by liberal parties, mostly centre-left.
days.source: CHES 2024 issue scores, derived (Rovny et al. 2025) · 87 parties in 27 countries

days.title: Fighting corruption
days.desc: Making the clean-up of politics a priority, with tougher rules on bribery, lobbying, party funding and conflicts of interest.
days.note: Almost every party says it wants a cleaner politics, so this lands close to the middle.
days.source: CHES 2024 issue scores, derived (Rovny et al. 2025) · 32 parties in 13 countries

days.title: Women's rights policies
days.desc: Laws and programmes aimed at gender equality, such as equal pay, paid parental leave, childcare support and protection from discrimination.
days.note: Equal pay and parental leave are championed mostly by left-leaning, socially liberal parties.
days.source: CHES 2024 issue scores, derived (Rovny et al. 2025) · 68 parties in 24 countries

days.title: Wealth redistribution
days.desc: Using taxes and transfers to move money from richer to poorer people, for example higher taxes on high earners paying for benefits or public services.
days.note: Taking from the wealthy to help everyone else is the classic left-wing idea. The parties behind it also tend to be socially liberal, so it sits low as well as far left.
days.source: CHES 2024 issue scores, derived (Rovny et al. 2025) · 33 parties in 20 countries

days.title: Environment over growth
days.desc: Protecting nature and limiting pollution, even at the cost of slower growth or fewer development projects.
days.note: Protecting nature even at some economic cost is a left and liberal position, and Green parties lead on it.
days.source: CHES 2024 issue scores, derived (Rovny et al. 2025) · 37 parties in 21 countries

days.title: Assimilation
days.desc: Newcomers are expected to adopt the majority language, customs and values, with the state encouraging a single shared national culture.
days.note: Expecting newcomers to adopt the local culture is backed mostly by authoritarian parties, with a mild lean to the right.
days.source: CHES 2024 issue scores, derived (Rovny et al. 2025) · 69 parties in 30 countries

days.title: Rural interests
days.desc: Policy that prioritises the countryside, for example farm support, rural services and protecting rural ways of life.
days.note: Putting the countryside first is mostly a traditional, authoritarian position, with a small lean right.
days.source: CHES 2024 issue scores, derived (Rovny et al. 2025) · 23 parties in 14 countries

days.title: Trade unions
days.desc: Backing organised labour and workers' collective rights, such as collective bargaining, the right to strike and union representation.
days.note: Backing for organised labour is a left-wing idea that sits about level on personal freedom.
days.source: Manifesto Project Dataset 2026a (Lehmann et al.), derived · 360 manifestos in 55 countries

days.title: Urban interests
days.desc: Policy that prioritises cities, such as public transport, housing and services for dense urban areas.
days.note: Putting cities first is a liberal position, with a mild lean to the right.
days.source: CHES 2024 issue scores, derived (Rovny et al. 2025) · 15 parties in 8 countries

days.title: Strong executive
days.desc: Presidents or prime ministers can make and carry out decisions quickly, with fewer checks from parliament or the courts.
days.note: Letting leaders act without heavy constraint is authoritarian at heart, and it appeals to parties across the economic spectrum.
days.source: CHES 2024 issue scores, derived (Rovny et al. 2025) · 34 parties in 16 countries

days.title: Human rights and freedoms
days.desc: Protecting personal freedoms, civil rights and the rule of law, such as free speech, fair trials and protection from arbitrary state action.
days.note: Parties that talk most about human rights are liberal, with almost no economic lean.
days.source: Manifesto Project Dataset 2026a (Lehmann et al.), derived · 360 manifestos in 49 countries

days.title: Liberal immigration
days.desc: Easier routes for people to move to a country to work, study or seek safety, with fewer caps and simpler visa rules.
days.note: Open-door parties lean left and are strongly liberal on personal freedom. It's one of the clearest low-and-left ideas.
days.source: CHES 2024 issue scores, derived (Rovny et al. 2025) · 17 parties in 12 countries

days.title: Free movement across borders
days.desc: People, goods, services and money can move freely between member countries, for example to work or study, without special permits.
days.note: Letting goods, services and workers move freely appeals to the centre and centre-right, with a lean liberal.
days.source: CHES 2024 issue scores, derived (Rovny et al. 2025) · 90 parties in 26 countries

days.title: Same-sex marriage
days.desc: Allowing couples of the same sex to marry, with the same legal rights as other married couples.
days.note: Like wider LGBTQ+ rights, this is a socially liberal idea with only a mild economic lean.
days.source: CHES 2024 issue scores, derived (Rovny et al. 2025) · 100 parties in 27 countries

days.title: Independent judiciary
days.desc: Judges decide cases free from pressure by politicians, with protected appointments and no government direction of rulings.
days.note: Almost every party says it backs independent courts, so this sits near the middle, leaning a little liberal.
days.source: CHES 2024 issue scores, derived (Rovny et al. 2025) · 130 parties in 27 countries

days.title: Leaving international unions
days.desc: Countries take back powers from shared bodies like the EU, to make their own laws, trade deals and border rules.
days.note: Taking powers back from shared bodies is backed by nationalist, authoritarian parties, mostly a bit right of centre.
days.source: CHES 2024 issue scores, derived (Rovny et al. 2025) · 35 parties in 20 countries

days.title: Limits on leaders
days.desc: Strong checks and balances, such as independent courts, a free press and term limits, so those in power cannot act unchecked.
days.note: Checks and balances are favoured by liberal parties, more often on the left.
days.source: CHES 2024 issue scores, derived (Rovny et al. 2025) · 19 parties in 12 countries

days.title: Nationalism
days.desc: Putting a nation's identity, interests and sovereignty first, including in trade, immigration and relations with other countries.
days.note: Putting the nation first is the signature of authoritarian parties, most of whom lean right on economics.
days.source: CHES 2024 issue scores, derived (Rovny et al. 2025) · 60 parties in 28 countries

days.title: LGBTQ+ rights
days.desc: Legal protection from discrimination and equal treatment in areas such as employment, housing, family law and healthcare.
days.note: Backed by socially liberal parties, mostly on the centre-left, so it sits low and a little left.
days.source: CHES 2024 issue scores, derived (Rovny et al. 2025) · 80 parties in 27 countries

days.title: Equality
days.desc: Fairer outcomes and treatment for all groups, through equal rights, anti-discrimination laws and support for those who start at a disadvantage.
days.note: Parties that talk about fairness and equal treatment lean left and liberal.
days.source: Manifesto Project Dataset 2026a (Lehmann et al.), derived · 360 manifestos in 50 countries

days.title: Public services first
days.desc: Putting money into health, education, transport and similar services before cutting taxes, even if that means keeping taxes higher.
days.note: Parties that put hospitals and schools ahead of tax cuts sit well to the left, and most are socially liberal too.
days.source: CHES 2024 issue scores, derived (Rovny et al. 2025) · 42 parties in 22 countries

days.title: Civil liberties first
days.desc: Strong limits on state power, such as protecting privacy, free speech and the rights of suspects, even if that makes fighting crime harder.
days.note: Putting freedoms ahead of security is a libertarian instinct. It leans left because left-wing parties are the ones leading on it today.
days.source: CHES 2024 issue scores, derived (Rovny et al. 2025) · 40 parties in 20 countries

days.title: Strict immigration limits
days.desc: Tight caps and controls on who may enter and settle, such as quotas, tougher visa rules and stronger border enforcement.
days.note: The parties pushing hardest for limits are strongly authoritarian, but they come from both sides on the economy. So it sits high up and only slightly right.
days.source: CHES 2024 issue scores, derived (Rovny et al. 2025) · 70 parties in 30 countries

days.title: Military strength
days.desc: Spending more on the armed forces and defence, and building up the country's ability to deter and fight.
days.note: Parties that give the armed forces a lot of attention lean right and a little authoritarian.
days.source: Manifesto Project Dataset 2026a (Lehmann et al.), derived · 360 manifestos in 54 countries

days.title: Deeper international union
days.desc: Member countries share more power in a common body, such as a joint budget or common laws, and give up some national control.
days.note: Pooling more power in a shared body is backed by centrist, liberal-leaning parties.
days.source: CHES 2024 issue scores, derived (Rovny et al. 2025) · 114 parties in 31 countries

days.title: Trade protectionism
days.desc: Using tariffs, quotas or subsidies to protect domestic industries and jobs from foreign competition.
days.note: This one splits the middle. Left parties protect jobs and nationalist right parties protect industry, so it lands near the centre line but high on the grid.
days.source: CHES 2024 issue scores, derived (Rovny et al. 2025) · 35 parties in 16 countries

days.title: Regulated markets
days.desc: Strong government rules on business, such as price controls and consumer protections, to steer markets towards public goals.
days.note: Strong rules on business are a left-wing instinct, and the parties behind them are mostly socially liberal.
days.source: CHES 2024 issue scores, derived (Rovny et al. 2025) · 28 parties in 17 countries

days.title: Anti-militarism
days.desc: Cutting military spending and weapons, and favouring peace, disarmament and diplomacy over military solutions.
days.note: Parties that stress peace and disarmament lean left and a little liberal.
days.source: Manifesto Project Dataset 2026a (Lehmann et al.), derived · 360 manifestos in 50 countries

days.title: Traditional morality
days.desc: Law and public life that uphold traditional family and moral values, for example on marriage, family life and public decency.
days.note: Parties that talk most about traditional values are strongly authoritarian and lean right.
days.source: Manifesto Project Dataset 2026a (Lehmann et al.), derived · 360 manifestos in 56 countries

days.title: Multiculturalism
days.desc: Different cultural, religious and ethnic groups keep their own traditions and identities within one society, with the state supporting this.
days.note: Parties that welcome many cultures living side by side lean left and liberal.
days.source: CHES 2024 issue scores, derived (Rovny et al. 2025) · 24 parties in 17 countries

days.title: Anti-establishment politics
days.desc: Presenting politics as a struggle between ordinary people and the political and economic elite, and promising to challenge it.
days.note: Attacking elites is a populist theme. It sits high on the grid and close to the middle on the economy because both left and right do it.
days.source: CHES 2024 issue scores, derived (Rovny et al. 2025) · 49 parties in 26 countries

days.title: Free trade
days.desc: Few or no tariffs or quotas, so goods and services can be bought and sold across borders with minimal government interference.
days.note: Open borders for goods and services means fewer state controls, which makes it right-leaning and liberal.
days.source: CHES 2024 issue scores, derived (Rovny et al. 2025) · 15 parties in 11 countries

days.title: Tough on crime
days.desc: Stronger policing and longer sentences to deter crime, even where that limits some individual freedoms or suspects' protections.
days.note: Harsher policing and sentences are pushed by authoritarian parties from across the economic spectrum, so it sits high and only a bit right.
days.source: CHES 2024 issue scores, derived (Rovny et al. 2025) · 55 parties in 27 countries

days.title: Expanding education
days.desc: More public spending on schools, universities and training, such as smaller classes, lower fees or more places.
days.note: Spending more on schools and universities is mildly left, and it's backed from across the spectrum.
days.source: Manifesto Project Dataset 2026a (Lehmann et al.), derived · 360 manifestos in 53 countries

days.title: Religion in politics
days.desc: Religious beliefs and institutions help shape laws and public policy, for example on family life, education or moral questions.
days.note: Parties that want faith to shape the law are strongly traditional, so it sits near the top. It has little to say about economics.
days.source: CHES 2024 issue scores, derived (Rovny et al. 2025) · 34 parties in 17 countries

days.title: International authority over security
days.desc: A union of countries sets shared foreign and defence policy, with common decisions on security instead of each country deciding alone.
days.note: Parties that want a shared foreign and defence policy lean slightly liberal, and they come from all along the economic line.
days.source: CHES 2024 issue scores, derived (Rovny et al. 2025) · 24 parties in 15 countries

days.title: Government sway over judges
days.desc: Elected governments have a say in appointing, promoting or overruling judges, so courts answer more directly to politicians.
days.note: Wanting politicians to have a say over courts is a strongly authoritarian stance, with a mild lean right.
days.source: CHES 2024 issue scores, derived (Rovny et al. 2025) · 12 parties in 8 countries

days.title: Centralised government
days.desc: Key decisions are made by the national government, with regions and local authorities following common national rules.
days.note: Parties that want decisions made nationally are strongly authoritarian, with little economic lean.
days.source: CHES 2024 issue scores, derived (Rovny et al. 2025) · 16 parties in 11 countries

days.title: Growth over environment
days.desc: Putting economic growth and jobs first, and easing environmental rules where they hold back industry or raise costs.
days.note: Putting the economy first is right-leaning. In practice the parties that do it are also traditional and authoritarian.
days.source: CHES 2024 issue scores, derived (Rovny et al. 2025) · 25 parties in 17 countries

days.title: Direct democracy
days.desc: Citizens vote directly on major issues, through referendums or citizen initiatives, instead of leaving them to elected representatives.
days.note: Letting the public decide big questions by referendum is mostly a populist idea. Populists sit high on the grid but all over the economic spectrum.
days.source: CHES 2024 issue scores, derived (Rovny et al. 2025) · 26 parties in 14 countries

days.title: Cosmopolitanism
days.desc: Seeing people as citizens of the world first, and valuing open borders, international cooperation and shared global rules over national interests.
days.note: Seeing yourself as a citizen of the world is a liberal, left-leaning outlook.
days.source: CHES 2024 issue scores, derived (Rovny et al. 2025) · 40 parties in 22 countries

days.title: Cutting taxes
days.desc: Lowering income, business or sales taxes, and accepting less government spending as a result.
days.note: Tax cuts are backed by the economic right, often alongside parties that favour traditional values. That pulls it a little way up the grid.
days.source: CHES 2024 issue scores, derived (Rovny et al. 2025) · 27 parties in 16 countries

days.title: Climate as top priority
days.desc: Making climate change the central issue of a party's campaign, ahead of other topics such as the economy or health.
days.note: Parties that put climate first are the Greens and their allies: clearly left and among the most libertarian on the grid.
days.source: CHES 2024 issue scores, derived (Rovny et al. 2025) · 30 parties in 20 countries

days.title: Redistribution as top priority
days.desc: Making the question of how much money the state moves from rich to poor the central issue of a party's campaign.
days.note: Putting inequality at the centre of politics is a left-wing habit, and the parties that do it are mostly socially liberal too.
days.source: CHES 2024 issue scores, derived (Rovny et al. 2025) · 36 parties in 21 countries

days.title: Accommodating Russia
days.desc: Favouring talks and better relations with Russia, and opposing sanctions or weapons for Ukraine, so that tensions ease.
days.note: Parties that want warmer ties with Moscow are mostly authoritarian, and many of them lean left on the economy, which puts this up and to the left.
days.source: CHES 2024 issue scores, derived (Rovny et al. 2025) · 28 parties in 14 countries

days.title: Representative democracy
days.desc: Elected representatives, not public referendums, make the main decisions on voters' behalf, weighing evidence and compromise.
days.note: Leaving big decisions to elected officials is the established view, so it sits close to the centre.
days.source: CHES 2024 issue scores, derived (Rovny et al. 2025) · 28 parties in 10 countries

days.title: Ethnic minority rights
days.desc: Extra legal protection and support for ethnic minority groups, such as anti-discrimination law, language rights or fair representation.
days.note: Extra protections for minorities are backed by left-leaning, socially liberal parties.
days.source: CHES 2024 issue scores, derived (Rovny et al. 2025) · 50 parties in 24 countries

days.title: Climate policy over growth
days.desc: Cutting emissions through measures like carbon pricing and clean-energy rules, even if it slows economic growth or raises costs.
days.note: Parties willing to accept slower growth for lower emissions lean left and liberal.
days.source: CHES 2024 issue scores, derived (Rovny et al. 2025) · 38 parties in 21 countries

days.title: Standing up to Russia
days.desc: Supporting sanctions on Russia, military and financial help for Ukraine, and a firm line against Russian influence in Europe.
days.note: Backing sanctions and support for Ukraine cuts across the usual divides. Its supporters sit just right of centre and slightly libertarian.
days.source: CHES 2024 issue scores, derived (Rovny et al. 2025) · 65 parties in 21 countries

days.title: Devolving power
days.desc: Moving decisions from the national government to regions and local authorities, such as over taxes, schools or policing.
days.note: Giving regions more say appeals to all kinds of parties, so it ends up close to the centre.
days.source: CHES 2024 issue scores, derived (Rovny et al. 2025) · 27 parties in 12 countries

days.title: Europe as top priority
days.desc: Making the EU and a country's place in it the central issue of a party's campaign, whether for or against.
days.note: Parties that talk most about the EU come from both sides, strong supporters and strong opponents, so they average out close to the middle.
days.source: CHES 2024 issue scores, derived (Rovny et al. 2025) · 25 parties in 14 countries

days.title: Immigration as top priority
days.desc: Making immigration the central issue of a party's campaign, ahead of other topics such as the economy or health.
days.note: The parties that campaign hardest on immigration are overwhelmingly authoritarian, so this sits near the top of the grid, a little right of centre.
days.source: CHES 2024 issue scores, derived (Rovny et al. 2025) · 51 parties in 28 countries

days.title: Green politics
days.desc: Putting the protection of the environment first, together with social justice, peace and decisions made close to the people affected.
days.note: Green parties are strongly left and the most libertarian of the families, which puts them in the bottom-left corner.
days.source: Global Party Survey 2019 (Norris), derived · 14 parties in 14 countries

days.title: Christian democracy
days.desc: Politics based on Christian social teaching: support for the family, local community and a welfare state, with a moderate approach to the economy.
days.note: Christian democratic parties back a market economy with a welfare safety net, and hold traditional views on family and morality. That makes them right of centre and fairly authoritarian.
days.source: Global Party Survey 2019 (Norris), derived · 14 parties in 12 countries

days.title: Patronage politics
days.desc: Giving jobs, contracts and benefits mainly to a party's own supporters and voters, instead of sharing them out equally among all citizens.
days.note: Parties that reward their own supporters are found across the economic spectrum, so this is near the middle horizontally. It sits well up the grid because these parties are mostly socially conservative.
days.source: Global Party Survey 2019 (Norris), derived · 205 parties in 87 countries

days.title: Liberalism
days.desc: Putting individual freedom first: free speech, the rule of law, open markets and limits on what government can do to people.
days.note: Liberal parties favour personal freedom and are a little right of centre on the economy. They sit in the libertarian half of the grid.
days.source: Global Party Survey 2019 (Norris), derived · 32 parties in 23 countries

days.title: Conservatism
days.desc: Valuing established institutions, tradition and gradual change over rapid reform, usually with a preference for lower taxes and a smaller state.
days.note: Conservative parties combine a market-friendly economy with traditional social values, which puts them in the upper right.
days.source: Global Party Survey 2019 (Norris), derived · 42 parties in 28 countries

days.title: Social democracy
days.desc: Keeping a market economy but using strong unions, taxes and public services to reduce inequality and give everyone a social safety net.
days.note: Social democratic parties want a bigger state and a stronger welfare system, and are mostly socially liberal. That puts them left of centre and a little below the middle.
days.source: Global Party Survey 2019 (Norris), derived · 41 parties in 31 countries

days.title: Undermining democratic norms
days.desc: Weakening checks on power, such as independent courts, a free press and a fair opposition, so that the governing party is harder to remove.
days.note: Parties that experts say weaken courts, media and opposition are some of the most authoritarian in the survey. They are spread evenly between economic left and right.
days.source: Global Party Survey 2019 (Norris), derived · 112 parties in 77 countries

days.title: Populism
days.desc: A style of politics that casts the 'pure people' against a corrupt elite and claims to speak for the people's will. Populists exist on both the left and the right.
days.note: Populist parties come from both left and right, so on average this lands about level horizontally. What they share is a style that treats elites as the enemy, which lifts it into the authoritarian half.
days.source: Global Party Survey 2019 (Norris), derived · 187 parties in 104 countries

days.title: Radical right
days.desc: Nativist and nationalist politics that wants far less immigration, defends a traditional national culture and distrusts the liberal establishment.
days.note: Radical right parties are strongly authoritarian but only mildly right on economics, and many support the welfare state, so they sit near the top but not far right.
days.source: Global Party Survey 2019 (Norris), derived · 21 parties in 20 countries

days.title: Socialism
days.desc: Common or public ownership of key industries and a far larger role for the state in the economy, in pursuit of equality.
days.note: The socialist and communist parties are the furthest left of the families here, and tend to be socially liberal too.
days.source: Global Party Survey 2019 (Norris), derived · 19 parties in 16 countries
